network.overall_strategy: Construct ten distinct reaction-node sequences using three pyruvate-supply branches, three chemically different reductive-amination branches, and one acetaldehyde Strecker branch. The two oxaloacetate branches are catalyst-dependent alternatives, not different carbon-fixation mechanisms. All alanine-forming reactions produce both L- and D-alanine; L-alanine is present, but enantiomeric enrichment is not claimed. The supplied review's two hydroxylamine equations are treated as one transformation, with sacrificial iron consumption and electron balance made explicit. Unsupported serine hydrogenolysis, sulfur-driven lactate photooxidation, acetaldehyde capture from pyruvate, and hydantoin chemistry are excluded. Additional ammonia-based aminations draw on Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003); their integration is explicitly conditional. These are ten graph routes, not ten independently demonstrated end-to-end syntheses. Numerical conditions identified as proposed are experimental screening specifications, not claimed published protocols or guaranteed productive operating windows. External feedstocks include oxaloacetate, hydroxylamine, acetaldehyde and HCN; their formation is outside this network boundary. Neutral parent formulas represent acid-base pools except where charged species are required for redox accounting. Stereo-unspecified aminonitrile and amide nodes represent racemic precursor pools. The single environment_formed value records a representative formation environment where more than one applies.

molecules.common_name: ferric hydroxide, formal hydrated Fe(III) sink

reactions.name: Awaruite-mediated hydrogen-dependent CO2 fixation to pyruvate
agents: awaruite, Ni3Fe, as a hydrogen-activating mineral catalyst

conditions.pressure: Proposed: 25 bar total initial gas pressure, H2:CO2 = 4:1
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 1-10 g/L freshly characterized awaruite, 16-72 h, initial room-temperature pH 9-10 before gas charging. Measure pH after CO2 uptake rather than assuming it remains alkaline. Use an anoxic, gas-retaining reactor. Quantify pyruvate against blanks and distinguish it from more abundant C1/C2 products. Filter mineral particles and cool promptly before downstream processing.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped, multistep surface reaction combines hydrogen activation, CO2 reduction and carbon-carbon bond formation. The detailed sequence to pyruvate is not established and is not presented as a proven Fischer-Tropsch mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Preiner et al. (2020) supports hydrogen-dependent mineral-mediated formation of metabolic intermediates, including pyruvate, near 373 K. Only one mineral implementation is included; the review's mineral combinations are not multiplied into presumed equivalent pyruvate-producing routes. The numerical loading, gas composition and residence-time window above are proposed rather than extracted experimental conditions. Mineral-specific pyruvate yield, catalyst history and reproducibility remain essential checks. Pyruvate is a minor product, so neither preparative selectivity nor sufficient concentration for subsequent chemistry is assumed.

reactions.name: Ferrous-ion-promoted oxaloacetate decarboxylation
agents: dissolved iron(II), acting as a Lewis-acid promoter

conditions.temperature: 350-353 K proposed; cited experimental benchmark is 343 K
conditions.pressure: Proposed: 10 bar in a closed aqueous mixing-zone analogue
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 0.1-5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.1-5 mM dissolved Fe(II), initial pH 5-7, 1-24 h with time-resolved sampling. Exclude oxygen and initially exclude sulfide, which would remove dissolved Fe(II). Avoid prolonged storage of the resulting pyruvate.

reactions.mechanism: Iron(II) coordinates the beta-keto-acid functionality, facilitates carbon-carbon bond cleavage and CO2 loss, and permits the resulting enol to tautomerize to pyruvate.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) supports iron-promoted oxaloacetate-to-pyruvate conversion at 343 K. The slightly warmer proposed window respects the requested hydrothermal range but is an extrapolation requiring kinetic verification. Oxaloacetate is an explicitly supplied precursor, not an internally generated carbon-fixation product. Sulfide precipitation, metal complexation and pyruvate decomposition must be controlled before transferring this stream to an amination stage.

reactions.name: Uncatalyzed aqueous oxaloacetate decarboxylation

conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 0.1-5 mM oxaloacetate, initial pH 4-6, 1-48 h. Use a shaded or sediment-covered aqueous pool analogue, with no intentionally added transition-metal catalyst. Follow oxaloacetate disappearance and pyruvate appearance separately. Transfer locally to a geothermal reaction zone only if pyruvate retention is demonstrated.

reactions.mechanism: The intrinsically labile beta-keto acid loses CO2 through an enol-forming decarboxylation, followed by tautomerization to pyruvate.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson (2021), as cited in the supplied review, supports a surface oxaloacetate-to-pyruvate connection. Ordinary beta-keto-acid chemistry also supports spontaneous decarboxylation without requiring a sulfur oxidant or UV excitation. The specific metal-free pH and residence-time window proposed here is not established by that citation and is a conditional implementation. This is a catalyst-free alternative to rxn_002, not an additional carbon-skeleton synthesis mechanism.

reactions.name: Iron-driven hydroxylamine conversion of pyruvate to racemic alanine
agents: native iron, explicitly consumed as a stoichiometric reductant
dissolved iron(II), as a coordination promoter

conditions.temperature: 350-353 K proposed; cited experimental benchmark is 343 K
conditions.pressure: Proposed: 10 bar in a closed aqueous reactor
conditions.catalyst: iron(II) coordination promoter; iron metal is not treated as a regenerated catalyst
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 0.01-1 mM pyruvate, 10-100 mM total hydroxylamine, 0.05-0.5 mol/L iron-metal inventory, initial pH 5-7, 4-48 h. Maintain anoxia and exclude sulfide carryover that could passivate iron. The explicit proton node supplies formal redox bookkeeping; actual proton activity is buffered and evolves during iron corrosion. Assay hydroxylamine loss, dissolved iron and both alanine enantiomers.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine condenses with pyruvate to an oxime-type intermediate. Reduction of the carbon-nitrogen functionality and cleavage of the nitrogen-oxygen bond give alanine. Formation of alanine from pyruvate and hydroxylamine requires four reducing equivalents per alanine molecule.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) supports iron-driven amino-acid formation from keto-acid precursors with hydroxylamine. Metallic iron oxidation to Fe(II) is included explicitly, correcting the redox-incomplete equations in the supplied review. Its two water-accounting variants are not counted as different pathways. The proposed temperature, concentrations and pressure are not a reproduced published protocol. Hydroxylamine availability, competing reduction of hydroxylamine to ammonia, and trace-level pyruvate capture are major limitations. No asymmetric catalyst is present, so both alanine enantiomers are outputs.

reactions.name: Ferrous-hydroxide-driven reductive amination with ammonia
agents: iron(II) hydroxide, consumed as a reductant rather than assumed to be catalytic

conditions.pressure: Proposed: 10 bar, closed anoxic aqueous system
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 0.01-1 mM pyruvate, 0.1-0.5 M total ammonia/ammonium, 0.05-0.2 mol/L freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2 inventory, initial pH 8-9.5, 24-168 h. Retain ammonia in the closed system. Remove sulfide before this branch because it changes the iron mineral assemblage. Measure iron oxidation states and solid phases rather than inferring them from alanine detection.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine or iminium intermediate with pyruvate. Oxidation of ferrous iron supplies the two electrons required for reduction to alanine. Hydrated ferric hydroxide represents the formal oxidized-iron sink in the atom and electron ledger.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative at the integrated-network level relative to the supplied review, but the reaction class has additional experimental support in Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003), 'Primordial reductive amination revisited', which investigated ferrous-hydroxide-supported reductive amination. It is included because ammonia is a chemically distinct nitrogen source that avoids reliance on hydroxylamine. The proposed loadings, performance at dilute pyruvate concentrations and natural co-location are not demonstrated here. Fe(OH)3 is a formal hydrated Fe(III) product, not a claim that a particular crystalline hydroxide was measured; oxyhydroxide or mixed-valence phases could require revised phase-specific bookkeeping.

reactions.name: Iron-sulfide and hydrogen-sulfide-supported reductive amination
agents: mackinawite, explicitly included as a consumed iron-sulfide phase

conditions.pressure: Proposed: 10 bar in a closed, sulfide-retaining aqueous reactor
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 0.01-1 mM pyruvate, 0.1-0.5 M total ammonia/ammonium, 0.05-0.2 mol/L FeS inventory, 0.01-0.1 M total dissolved sulfide, initial pH 6.5-8.5, 24-168 h. Establish this as a separate sulfide-rich reactor rather than adding sulfide to the hydroxylamine/iron-metal branch. Quantify pyrite formation, competing sulfur phases and alanine production.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-derived imine formation is followed by reduction coupled to conversion of monosulfide and dissolved sulfide into disulfide in pyrite. Sulfur oxidation supplies reducing equivalents without molecular oxygen.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative at the integrated-network level relative to the supplied review, with additional reaction-class support from Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) for iron-sulfide-associated reductive amination. This branch tests an ammonia-based alternative in a geochemically different reducing assemblage. The explicit FeS/H2S-to-FeS2 ledger avoids treating mineral reducing power as unlimited catalysis. However, the proposed system must demonstrate coupled pyrite and alanine formation: pyrite-forming thermodynamics alone does not establish reaction rate, selectivity or the identity of the operative reductant. Surface passivation and competing sulfide chemistry are key limitations.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde Strecker formation of alaninonitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in a gas-retaining pore or closed laboratory analogue
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 10-100 mM acetaldehyde, 10-100 mM total HCN/cyanide, 0.1-0.5 M total ammonia/ammonium, initial pH 8-9, 1-7 days. Use covered or sediment-shielded water rather than assuming aminonitrile survival under continuous strong UV. Measure acetaldehyde and HCN losses as well as aminonitrile formation. Feedstock concentration and volatile retention are prerequisites, not assumed consequences of wet-dry cycling.

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde and ammonia form an imine/iminium pool; cyanide addition gives racemic 2-aminopropanenitrile. Water is the net condensation coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Classical Strecker chemistry supports this carbon-nitrogen bond-forming sequence (Strecker, 1850), while Patel et al. (2015) supports aminonitrile precursors within prebiotic cyanosulfidic chemistry. The proposed environmental concentrations and residence time are not attributed to either paper as measured protocols. Acetaldehyde is supplied directly, avoiding an unverified pyruvate-decarboxylation and volatile-capture step. Competing cyanohydrin formation may occur, but a separate productive cyanohydrin pathway is not asserted.

reactions.name: Acid-catalyzed hydration of alaninonitrile to alaninamide
agents: aqueous acid, providing regenerated proton-transfer catalysis

conditions.pressure: Proposed: 10 bar, sufficient to retain liquid water over this temperature range
conditions.other: Proposed screening window: 1-50 mM aminonitrile, initial room-temperature pH 1-2, 24-168 h with intermediate sampling. Use an acidic, locally connected subsurface geothermal compartment; do not assume transport through the open ocean. Remove or quantify residual cyanide and ammonia before acidification. The amide may be transient and need not be isolated.

reactions.mechanism: Protonation activates the nitrile toward water addition. Proton transfers and tautomerization convert the hydrated nitrile into alaninamide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) supports the aminonitrile-to-amino-acid relationship, and sequential nitrile hydration followed by amide hydrolysis is established Strecker chemistry. The supplied review does not establish rapid neutral hydrolysis at ambient temperature, so that claim is not adopted. The hotter acidic implementation is a proposed geochemical extrapolation rather than a verified protocol from Patel et al. The productive hydration rate must be measured against decomposition, and mineral neutralization could prevent the required acidity.

reactions.name: Alanine release by complete alaninamide hydrolysis
agents: aqueous acid, providing regenerated proton-transfer catalysis

conditions.other: Continue the acidic hydrolysis stage for a proposed total residence time of 24-336 h, initial room-temperature pH 1-2, with time-resolved analysis. Quantify residual amide and free alanine independently; amide formation alone is not target formation. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium under these conditions but is represented by its neutral parent formula. Cool promptly after productive hydrolysis to limit further decomposition.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the protonated amide carbonyl. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate cleaves the carbon-nitrogen bond, releasing the carboxylic-acid amino-acid pool and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Complete aminonitrile hydrolysis is the alanine-producing endpoint associated with the precursor chemistry of Patel et al. (2015) and classical Strecker synthesis. This node explicitly requires amide cleavage rather than treating hydration as completed amino-acid synthesis. The proposed geothermal residence time is not a demonstrated prebiotic yield claim. Full conversion, alanine survival and maintenance of acidity are the branch's principal kinetic and environmental bottlenecks. Because the precursor pool is racemic, both L- and D-alanine are produced.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation followed by hydroxylamine/iron amination
pathways.description: CO2 and H2 supply pyruvate on awaruite, followed by sacrificial-iron reduction with externally supplied hydroxylamine. Supported reaction classes are connected conditionally; dilute-product capture and compatible staging remain unproven.

pathways.name: Iron-promoted oxaloacetate decarboxylation followed by hydroxylamine amination
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate forms pyruvate with Fe(II), followed by iron-driven hydroxylamine conversion. This has the closest alignment with the iron-mediated chemistry emphasized in the supplied review.

pathways.name: Surface oxaloacetate decarboxylation followed by hydroxylamine amination
pathways.description: Catalyst-free surface decarboxylation supplies pyruvate to a locally connected, warmer iron-containing compartment. Product retention and pH adjustment must be demonstrated.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation followed by ferrous-hydroxide/ammonia amination
pathways.description: Mineral-generated pyruvate enters an ammonia-based reductive-amination stage. This avoids hydroxylamine but depends on the conditional ferrous-hydroxide implementation and verification of its oxidized mineral products.

pathways.name: Iron-promoted oxaloacetate decarboxylation followed by ferrous-hydroxide amination
pathways.description: Oxaloacetate-derived pyruvate is transferred to a more alkaline ammonia/ferrous-hydroxide assemblage. Iron precipitation and ammonia retention require explicit staging.

pathways.name: Surface oxaloacetate decarboxylation followed by ferrous-hydroxide amination
pathways.description: An uncatalyzed pyruvate supply branch feeds the conditional ammonia/ferrous-hydroxide reaction after local heating and alkalinity adjustment.

pathways.name: CO2 fixation followed by sulfide-associated ammonia amination
pathways.description: Pyruvate generated on awaruite is separated from the fixation mineral before entering a distinct FeS/H2S-rich ammonia reactor. Coupling of sulfur oxidation to alanine production requires verification.

pathways.name: Iron-promoted oxaloacetate decarboxylation followed by sulfide-associated amination
pathways.description: Fe(II)-promoted decarboxylation supplies pyruvate before deliberate transition to a sulfide-rich mineral assemblage. This is a staged process, not an assumption that soluble Fe(II) and concentrated sulfide remain compatible.

pathways.name: Surface oxaloacetate decarboxylation followed by sulfide-associated amination
pathways.description: Surface-generated pyruvate feeds a locally connected sulfide-bearing hydrothermal compartment. This combines a catalyst-free supply variant with the conditional FeS/H2S ammonia-reduction branch.

pathways.name: Acetaldehyde Strecker synthesis followed by complete staged hydrolysis
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde, ammonia and HCN form racemic alaninonitrile in a protected surface solution. Acidic geothermal hydration forms alaninamide, and subsequent complete amide hydrolysis releases racemic alanine, including the L target. Volatile retention, acidity maintenance and measured completion of both hydrolysis stages are required.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Preiner et al. (2020) and Muchowska et al. (2019) provide relevant experimental support for the constituent transformations. Both reactions conserve atoms and charge with the supplied coefficients. The hydroxylamine step correctly requires four reducing electrons per alanine. The principal uncertainty is whether the fixation stage delivers usable pyruvate concentrations under conditions compatible with subsequent iron-mediated amination. Racemic production satisfies the stated L-alanine-presence claim.
suggestions: Specify awaruite preparation and loading, gas pressures, pH, temperature and residence time, distinguishing the Preiner protocol from proposed screening conditions.
Define the interstage handling and measure pyruvate survival, concentration and alanine yield in the actual fixation-product mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-supported route within the declared feedstock boundary. Ferrous-ion-promoted oxaloacetate decarboxylation and hydroxylamine/iron conversion of pyruvate to alanine align with Muchowska et al. (2019). The intermediates and reducing-equivalent accounting are appropriate. Compatible mild hydrothermal operation is plausible, although the network does not supply a complete sequential protocol. No intrinsically invalid reaction is identified.
suggestions: Specify the initial dissolved Fe2+ inventory, Fe0 loading, pH, temperature, reagent concentrations and addition sequence.
Measure sequential oxaloacetate-to-pyruvate-to-alanine conversion, including competing decomposition and hydroxylamine consumption.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Uncatalyzed aqueous decarboxylation of the beta-keto-acid functionality in oxaloacetate is chemically sound, and the downstream amination has relevant experimental support. The uncatalyzed surface step is a reasonable chemical generalization, but should not automatically be treated as the exact Ritson (2021) experiment. The principal network-level gap is an unspecified physical transfer of pyruvate to the iron-containing reaction environment, with unknown dilution and survival.
suggestions: Establish the uncatalyzed decarboxylation rate and pyruvate yield at the proposed surface pH and temperature.
Specify a physical transfer mechanism, residence time and concentration budget for delivering pyruvate to the amination stage.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sequence is stoichiometrically valid. Oxidation of two Fe(II) equivalents supplies the two electrons needed for ammonia-based reductive amination. Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) is cited as precedent, but the supplied material does not establish the exact conditions or performance of this integrated sequence. The formal Fe(III) hydroxide sink is acceptable bookkeeping, not evidence that productive reduction outcompetes passivation or other reactions.
suggestions: Provide the relevant Huber and Wächtershäuser experimental conditions and distinguish them from the proposed Fe(OH)2 implementation.
Test actual fixation effluent in the amination stage, specifying ammonia concentration, pH, iron phase, residence time and iron oxidation-state changes.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pyruvate-supply reaction is well founded and the ammonia-amination equation has correct electron accounting. The main uncertainty lies in the productive operating window for rxn_005, rather than conservation or precursor identity. Dissolved ferrous-ion conditions for decarboxylation and a reactive ferrous-hydroxide suspension need not be identical; their connection requires explicit pH and mineral-phase control. The conditional integration claim is appropriate.
suggestions: Specify how the decarboxylation mixture is brought into the pH and mineral conditions required for ammonia-based amination.
Report alanine yield alongside iron oxidation-state and precipitate measurements, with the exact supporting literature protocol.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both net transformations are chemically plausible and balanced. Confidence is limited by the combination of unspecified pyruvate delivery and conditional Fe(OH)2/ammonia amination. A surface-derived solution could reach a suitable heated, anoxic mineral environment, but the network supplies neither a physical transfer model nor a demonstrated concentration and residence-time budget. These are implementation uncertainties, not an objection to the environment ordering.
suggestions: Quantify pyruvate production, transport losses and delivery concentration under a specified physical setting.
Demonstrate ammonia-based amination using the transported solution and a characterized Fe(OH)2 phase under literature-matched or independently validated conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfur redox bookkeeping is valid: conversion of FeS and H2S to FeS2 can provide the two reducing electrons required per alanine. Nevertheless, balanced pyrite formation does not establish efficient coupling to ammonia-based amination. The Huber and Wächtershäuser citation provides a relevant lead, but exact experimental correspondence is unspecified. Integration also requires controlling sulfide exposure of the upstream metal catalyst and establishing adequate pyruvate delivery.
suggestions: Specify mineral retention or interstage transfer before sulfide addition, or demonstrate that the fixation catalyst tolerates the proposed exposure.
Document the supporting amination protocol and measure alanine yield, sulfide consumption and pyrite formation under the proposed conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ferrous-ion-promoted oxaloacetate decarboxylation supplies a credible pyruvate precursor. The subsequent sulfide-associated amination is balanced and has cited precedent, but its exact mineral phases, solution speciation and selective coupling remain insufficiently documented here. Ferrous-ion carryover can change FeS precipitation and the available sulfide inventory. These effects require characterization rather than an assumption that all hydrothermal iron conditions are interchangeable.
suggestions: Account for Fe2+ carryover, FeS precipitation and H2S/HS- speciation when defining the amination mixture.
Provide literature-matched or directly measured alanine yields with characterized mackinawite and an identified oxidized sulfur/mineral endpoint.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route has a valid carbon skeleton progression and no conservation violation. Its weaker points are the unquantified delivery of surface-produced pyruvate and the condition-dependent sulfide/ammonia amination. The supplied citation does not by itself establish productive operation with the proposed feed solution and mineral assemblage. L-alanine would be present if amination succeeds; the racemic outcome is not a target failure.
suggestions: Specify the hydrological or other physical connection and demonstrate sufficient pyruvate survival and concentration.
Define and test temperature, pressure, pH, ammonia concentration, sulfide speciation and mineral phases for productive reductive amination.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Classical Strecker chemistry supports alaninonitrile formation, and sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis form a valid route to racemic alanine. Patel et al. (2015) supports the broader aminonitrile-precursor framework, but should not automatically be cited as validation of this particular acid-hydrothermal protocol. The designation 'complete' hydrolysis requires kinetic evidence. Acidity, residence times, volatile-feedstock retention and aminonitrile survival during transfer are unspecified.
suggestions: Specify Strecker-stage pH, concentrations and retention or replenishment of acetaldehyde, HCN and ammonia.
Define the acid source, temperature, residence time and physical transfer setting for the hydrolysis stages.
Measure nitrile, amide and alanine over time to establish complete hydrolysis, distinguishing published conditions from proposed environmental implementation.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid: the molecule and reaction nodes are sufficient, IDs are used consistently, and the graph has no isolated subgraphs. All nine reactions pass the supplied atom/charge check with modest coefficients; there are no conservation violations. The formal acid-base pools and hydrated Fe(III) sink are acceptable representations, subject to actual solution and mineral speciation. The pathways provide credible routes to L-alanine as a component of racemic alanine, without establishing enantiomeric enrichment or isolation. Literature alignment is strongest for the iron-promoted oxaloacetate/hydroxylamine route and for the constituent Strecker transformations. The supplied review's schematic equations are not independent conservation evidence, and its broad hydrolysis descriptions do not establish useful rates under unspecified conditions. The main limitations are missing operating specifications, unquantified interstage transfer and concentration budgets, and conditional implementation of rxn_005 and rxn_006. Broad environment labels and references to proposed screening conditions do not supply an executable protocol. Problematic-reaction lists identify evidence, kinetic or operating-condition gaps, not mass-balance failures. This assessment concerns the complete network rather than its best route; no credit or penalty is assigned for feedstock choice, hub count, route count or environment ordering. External-feedstock formation is appropriately outside the declared boundary. At 0.84 overall confidence, the network is not approved under the required 0.90 threshold.
